frictionVectors.title: Morocco-Western Sahara rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Algeria's support for the Polisario Front keeps borders with Morocco closed and complicates regional energy, transport, and security cooperation.

frictionVectors.title: European gas diversification
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains dependent on Algerian gas, but long-term diversification and renewable investment could reduce Algiers' bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: US and European backing for the corridor increases Angola's infrastructure leverage but also places its transport and mineral gateways inside wider competition with China.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: Oil still dominates fiscal capacity, leaving Luanda exposed to production declines, foreign technical dependence, and volatile prices despite diversification efforts.

frictionVectors.title: Niger border and pipeline tensions
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger remain strained, threatening trade routes and the operating environment around the Niger-Benin oil export corridor.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-controlled logistics exposure
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou's importance depends on foreign-backed port, road, and pipeline infrastructure, creating commercial leverage that can constrain national policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers partnership renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has secured a stronger position in diamond marketing and revenues, but maintaining production, investment, and market access remains a delicate balance.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral competition
frictionVectors.details: Interest in copper, nickel, and other critical minerals brings capital and infrastructure opportunities while raising pressure to preserve domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector control and leakage
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking tighter state oversight of industrial and artisanal gold, but insecurity and informal networks continue to divert production and revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security partnership
frictionVectors.details: The shift away from French influence toward Russian-backed security cooperation may increase regime autonomy, but it risks opaque concessions, civilian harm, and dependence on external military support.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC and Rwanda spillover
frictionVectors.details: Security tensions around eastern DRC and strained relations with Rwanda threaten border commerce and regional transport links.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking foreign capital for nickel and other minerals, but limited financing options could produce contracts that weaken long-term state control.

frictionVectors.title: Port competition and external financing
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed investment in maritime infrastructure strengthens Cabo Verde's connectivity but increases exposure to competing European, Chinese, and security interests.

frictionVectors.title: Water and energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago remains dependent on imported fuel, food, and desalination inputs, leaving sovereignty sensitive to shipping costs and external supply disruptions.

highlights: Pipeline and ports anchor export power

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone conflict and border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency in the Northwest and Southwest continues to undermine transport, taxation, and state control over productive areas near Nigeria.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-linked resource infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, mining, timber, and Chinese-financed infrastructure remain central to growth, but opaque concessions and debt-linked projects constrain domestic value capture.

highlights: Russian security ties shape mining access

frictionVectors.title: Security-for-minerals dependence
frictionVectors.details: Russian security cooperation and associated mining interests provide regime support while raising concerns over opaque gold and diamond concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Peripheral border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Instability along the Sudan, Chad, and DRC frontiers disrupts trade corridors and leaves the government dependent on external military and humanitarian logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan spillover and refugee pressure
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in Sudan drives refugee flows, arms trafficking, and cross-border insecurity, stretching state capacity in eastern Chad.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and foreign oil dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's export system relies on the Cameroon pipeline and foreign technical and financial partners, limiting control over revenue flows and infrastructure decisions.

highlights: Mayotte dispute remains a sovereignty pressure point
Maritime and infrastructure capacity slowly expanding

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and maritime jurisdiction
frictionVectors.details: France's control of Mayotte limits Comoros' effective sovereignty claims and complicates access to surrounding maritime resources. The dispute also sustains diplomatic friction and migration-related tensions.

frictionVectors.title: External dependence for infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Ports, energy, telecommunications, and transport remain heavily dependent on foreign financing and contractors. Limited domestic fiscal capacity reduces bargaining power over strategic assets.

highlights: Critical minerals remain the core sovereignty test
Eastern conflict undermines territorial and resource control

frictionVectors.title: Eastern armed conflict and cross-border influence
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and wider regional rivalries continues to weaken state authority around mineral-rich eastern provinces. Security dependence on external partners risks trading short-term support for reduced strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and copper value capture
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and state-linked investors dominate financing, processing, and export channels for critical minerals. Contract renegotiations and local-content efforts have improved leverage but have not yet secured broad domestic value capture.

highlights: Oil revenue still anchors state finances

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains highly exposed to offshore oil production, foreign operators, and volatile prices. Limited diversification weakens the government's ability to convert resource income into durable sovereign capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, rail, and industrial projects provide essential connectivity but increase dependence on external capital and contractors. Debt-service pressures can constrain independent infrastructure policy.

highlights: Abidjan is consolidating as a regional logistics hub
Local processing is improving resource leverage

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire has expanded domestic processing and regulatory control, but farmers and the state remain exposed to foreign buyers, price swings, and sustainability requirements set abroad.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security and regional spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability in the Sahel continue to pressure northern border infrastructure and security spending. External security partnerships remain useful but create persistent questions about strategic autonomy.

highlights: Port geography delivers leverage but limits autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military-base concentration
frictionVectors.details: US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military presences generate revenue and diplomatic weight but make Djibouti's sovereignty vulnerable to great-power rivalry. Security guarantees are closely tied to continued external basing.

frictionVectors.title: Ports, debt, and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's infrastructure economy depends heavily on external operators, financing, and Ethiopian transit demand. The government retains formal control, but debt exposure and competing port corridors constrain its room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Egypt retains control over strategic assets but remains reliant on IMF programs, Gulf capital, and foreign currency support. Debt servicing and privatization pressures can reduce policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Nile dam dispute
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains Egypt's central resource-security concern. Cairo continues diplomatic and security pressure while seeking binding rules for Nile-water management.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining oil and gas production is weakening state revenues while offshore projects remain dependent on international operators, technology, and investment.

frictionVectors.title: Regional gas infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Equatorial Guinea seeks to preserve its LNG hub through imported and regional gas, increasing exposure to neighboring suppliers and external energy companies.

frictionVectors.title: Mining partner dependence
frictionVectors.details: Copper, gold, and zinc operations provide foreign exchange but rely heavily on external firms, specialized equipment, and export routes. This limits the depth of Eritrea's practical control over mineral value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea strategic pressure
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to the conflict around the Red Sea attract competing regional and international interests. Asmara prioritizes autonomy and restricts outside access, but remains exposed to maritime-security shifts.

highlights: Sugar and timber remain export anchors

frictionVectors.title: South African gateway dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies on South Africa for trade corridors, energy links, finance, and market access. This limits sovereign leverage over infrastructure and exposes the economy to South African disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: SACU revenue vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Customs receipts and regional trade arrangements remain crucial to public finances. Any slowdown in Southern African imports or reform of SACU distributions would sharply constrain fiscal autonomy.

highlights: Debt restructuring limits room to maneuver

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD expands Ethiopia's control over domestic electricity generation but continues to generate acute tensions with Egypt and Sudan. Disagreement over filling, drought management, and operating rules remains unresolved.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-finance and corridor exposure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, external budget support, and reliance on Djibouti-linked trade routes constrain Ethiopia's strategic autonomy. Gulf, Chinese, and Western actors compete for influence over logistics, energy, and telecommunications infrastructure.

highlights: Military transition tightens state control over strategic assets
Oil and manganese remain anchored to foreign capital

frictionVectors.title: Resource Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater local participation and fiscal returns from oil, manganese, and infrastructure projects. Disputes with established foreign operators could slow investment.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Logistics Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-linked operators remain important to Libreville and mineral-export logistics, limiting Gabon's operational autonomy despite stronger political oversight.

highlights: Stable civilian rule preserves donor-backed economic access
Senegal remains central to trade and security connectivity

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese Trade Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia's narrow geography and reliance on Senegalese transport corridors constrain independent control of trade routes and energy supplies.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Energy Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Banjul's port modernization and electricity expansion depend heavily on external finance, leaving infrastructure priorities exposed to donor and investor conditions.

highlights: Debt restructuring strengthens fiscal discipline but narrows policy space
Gold remains dominant as lithium and oil attract strategic competition

frictionVectors.title: Mining Sovereignty Gap
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and offshore capital remain deeply embedded in gold and emerging lithium value chains, while illegal mining continues to damage land and water governance.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and Creditor Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt-restructuring commitments and IMF-supported reforms constrain spending choices and reduce room for Ghana to impose more aggressive local-processing requirements.

highlights: Junta leverages bauxite and Simandou to expand state bargaining power
Mineral infrastructure is increasingly tied to foreign strategic capital

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Foreign-Control Risk
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore corridor can transform Guinea's fiscal position, but Chinese-linked and other international investors retain major influence over rail, port, and mine development.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Transitional Governance
frictionVectors.details: The junta's centralized decision-making may improve negotiating leverage while weakening transparency, community consent, and accountability over resource contracts.

highlights: Cashew dependence leaves the economy exposed to external price and buyer power
Political fragility limits independent control of ports and security

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Value-Chain Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign traders and processors capture substantial influence over the cashew economy, while limited domestic processing leaves Bissau vulnerable to price shocks and export bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Security Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and suspected transnational trafficking networks increase the role of external security and commercial actors around the port, reducing sovereign oversight.

highlights: Port and Mineral Sovereignty Under Pressure

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy external financing for rail, roads, and energy infrastructure limits Nairobi's policy autonomy. Chinese, Gulf, Western, and multilateral lenders compete for influence over strategic logistics assets.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and Critical-Mineral Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu corridor and emerging mineral opportunities attract outside capital while raising concerns over land rights, environmental safeguards, and whether local value capture will match national resource ambitions.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project Asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports provide essential revenue and leverage, but the country remains highly dependent on South African infrastructure, markets, and project financing. Delays and disputes can expose the imbalance in negotiating power.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Energy Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Export manufacturing and electricity supply are vulnerable to external market preferences and regional grid constraints. Limited domestic industrial capacity keeps Lesotho exposed to decisions made outside its borders.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, and other resource concessions remain central to growth but can deliver limited domestic value when taxation, local processing, and community protections are weak. The government faces pressure to renegotiate terms without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Rail, Port, and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed mining operations rely on dedicated rail and port corridors, giving investors significant influence over national logistics. Liberia is balancing Western, Chinese, and regional commercial interests while seeking stronger state oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Control of Oil Institutions
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to use oil production, export terminals, and budget flows as bargaining tools. Foreign commercial and diplomatic actors reinforce fragmentation by cultivating separate access channels.

frictionVectors.title: Externalized Security Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Turkish, Russian-linked, and other foreign security relationships shape access to bases, airfields, and strategic corridors. This limits Libya's sovereign control over critical infrastructure and complicates national reunification.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and Cobalt Value Capture
frictionVectors.details: Large mining projects attract foreign capital and technology but leave Madagascar exposed to commodity cycles, imported inputs, and limited domestic processing. Fiscal and environmental disputes can quickly become sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Weak transport, power, and port infrastructure increases reliance on external operators and lenders. Strategic mining and agricultural exports therefore remain vulnerable to disruptions and foreign negotiating leverage.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and Creditor Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and foreign-exchange shortages constrain policy autonomy, while IMF-backed reforms shape fuel, subsidy, and public-investment decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Minerals Governance
frictionVectors.details: Prospective uranium, graphite, and rare-earth projects could diversify exports, but limited state capacity raises risks of opaque concessions and weak local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian military personnel and political backing has increased strategic dependence while complicating relations with Western partners and neighboring states.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-Sector Control and Conflict
frictionVectors.details: The state is seeking a larger share of gold revenues, but insecurity, informal mining, and contested access routes continue to limit effective sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Greater Tortue Ahmeyim Governance
frictionVectors.details: Offshore gas production with Senegal offers major fiscal upside, but cross-border revenue management, local-content demands, and project delays remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily dependent on foreign-linked mining capital, rail capacity, and port logistics, limiting domestic control over the full export chain.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Diego Garcia
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago remains tied to negotiations over the long-term military use of Diego Garcia and broader Indian Ocean security.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Competition
frictionVectors.details: Investment from India, China, Gulf states, and Western partners strengthens infrastructure options but creates pressure to balance competing strategic interests.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Contest
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control and development of the territory strengthen its economic position, but sovereignty claims continue to generate diplomatic, legal, and investment risks.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Green-Hydrogen Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Renewable-energy and desalination expansion can improve strategic autonomy, yet major projects still require foreign capital, technology, and long-term export demand.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign LNG Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The offshore LNG sector relies heavily on foreign capital, technology, and security partnerships. Insurgent violence in Cabo Delgado continues to constrain Maputo's control over the resource corridor.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Large infrastructure and energy projects increase external financing exposure, limiting fiscal autonomy despite expected LNG revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Frontier Energy Ownership
frictionVectors.details: Major offshore oil discoveries and green-hydrogen projects could transform state revenues, but foreign operators retain substantial control over capital, technology, and project execution.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Competition among Western, Chinese, and Gulf investors for uranium and other minerals is strengthening Namibia's bargaining position while raising pressure over local processing and environmental safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The military-led government is seeking greater control over uranium and other extractive assets while reducing French influence. Renegotiation risks production disruptions and investor flight.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Closer security cooperation with Russia provides an alternative to Western partnerships but creates new dependence and does not resolve jihadist threats or border insecurity.

frictionVectors.title: Upstream Control and Capital Flight
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies remain central to upstream investment, while theft, contract uncertainty, and weak infrastructure reduce Nigeria's ability to capture full value from its resources.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and Refining Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: New domestic refining capacity could reduce import dependence, but pipeline vandalism, financing constraints, and foreign technology requirements continue to limit energy sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's position as a mineral-trading and processing hub faces persistent scrutiny over alleged links between regional armed groups and supply chains originating in eastern DRC.

frictionVectors.title: External Security and Aid Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign aid, investment, and security partnerships support Rwanda's development model but give external actors influence over its regional posture and strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Offshore petroleum prospects attract external interest, but limited commercial discoveries and state capacity constrain São Tomé and Príncipe’s bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Fishing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and weak maritime surveillance challenge control over fisheries, while outside partners remain important for patrol and port support.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Operator Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater state participation and local value capture from offshore oil and gas projects, creating friction with international operators and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Mauritania Offshore Interdependence
frictionVectors.details: The shared Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas project requires sustained Senegal-Mauritania coordination, leaving revenue, infrastructure, and maritime management exposed to bilateral tensions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fisheries Access
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles retains leverage through tuna licensing and fisheries diplomacy, but dependence on foreign fleets limits full control over marine resources.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean Competition
frictionVectors.details: Port, surveillance, and maritime-security partnerships draw interest from India, China, and Western states, forcing Victoria to balance sovereignty concerns against infrastructure needs.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dominance
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore, rutile, and other mining operations remain heavily dependent on foreign capital and expertise, limiting domestic control over pricing and value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Concession and Community Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Land access, environmental impacts, and revenue-sharing disputes around mining projects can generate friction between communities, the state, and foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil and Security Gap
frictionVectors.details: Emerging offshore petroleum ambitions are constrained by insurgency, fragmented federal authority, and limited maritime enforcement, increasing reliance on foreign security and investment partners.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Coastline Rivalries
frictionVectors.details: Competing Turkish, Gulf, Ethiopian, and regional interests in ports and maritime access intersect with the Somaliland dispute, making infrastructure a direct sovereignty flashpoint.

frictionVectors.title: LOGISTICS AND GRID DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Chronic electricity, rail, and port constraints limit South Africa’s ability to control and beneficiate its mineral exports. Private investment and foreign technology are increasingly important to stabilize strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL BENEFICIATION PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater local processing of platinum-group metals, manganese, and other critical minerals, while foreign buyers and mining companies resist costly restrictions and export controls.

frictionVectors.title: SUDAN EXPORT CORRIDOR
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan’s oil exports depend on pipelines and Port Sudan infrastructure exposed to Sudan’s civil war. Disruptions, transit bargaining, and opaque revenue arrangements sharply reduce Juba’s effective control over its principal resource.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL OIL AND SECURITY ACTORS
frictionVectors.details: Foreign oil firms, neighboring states, and security patrons retain substantial influence over production, transport, and political bargaining. Limited diversification leaves the state vulnerable to external pressure.

highlights: Gold and ports become strategic prizes

frictionVectors.title: GOLD WAR ECONOMY
frictionVectors.details: Competing military networks and foreign-linked traders exploit gold production and smuggling to finance the conflict. This diverts resource revenue away from civilian institutions and deepens external dependence.

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA INFRASTRUCTURE RIVALRY
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and associated logistics corridors are contested assets amid regional competition involving Gulf, Egyptian, Russian, and other outside interests. War damage and political fragmentation undermine sovereign management of trade infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR CONCESSIONS
frictionVectors.details: Foreign participation in ports, railways, and trade corridors is helping Tanzania expand regional connectivity but has prompted scrutiny over concession terms, strategic control, and long-term revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: LNG LOCAL-CONTENT BALANCE
frictionVectors.details: Prospective LNG development could strengthen state revenues and energy security, yet negotiations with international investors remain sensitive over fiscal terms, domestic processing, environmental safeguards, and local participation.

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEPENDENCE AND FOREIGN OPERATORS
frictionVectors.details: Lomé’s role as a Gulf of Guinea transshipment and Sahel trade hub brings revenue and strategic relevance, but reliance on foreign capital and operators limits direct national control over critical logistics.

frictionVectors.title: NORTHERN SECURITY SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability across Burkina Faso’s border threaten roads, agricultural supply chains, and state access to northern regions. External security partnerships are becoming more important as domestic capacity is stretched.

frictionVectors.title: EU MIGRATION AND FINANCIAL LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: European funding and migration cooperation give Brussels substantial influence over Tunisia's fiscal and security choices. Domestic resistance remains strong against perceived external conditionality.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY AND PHOSPHATE VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on imported energy and declining phosphate output constrain economic sovereignty. Investment and market access remain exposed to European and international financing conditions.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP FINANCING AND HUMAN RIGHTS
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains central to Kampala's resource strategy but faces sustained criticism from Western governments, civil society, and lenders over land acquisition and environmental impacts.

frictionVectors.title: CHINESE INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese contractors and finance remain important for transport and energy infrastructure, increasing Kampala's room for maneuver while creating longer-term debt and procurement dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL MINERALS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using renewed interest in copper and cobalt to seek greater processing, tax, and infrastructure benefits from multinational investors. Competition among Western, Chinese, and Gulf-linked firms remains intense.

frictionVectors.title: IMF AND CREDITOR CONDITIONALITY
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF support stabilize the state but limit fiscal flexibility. External creditors retain influence over public investment, mining policy, and subsidy decisions.

frictionVectors.title: CHINESE MINING DOMINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms hold a major position in Zimbabwe's lithium and other mineral sectors, providing capital and infrastructure while raising concerns over limited domestic value capture and transparency.

frictionVectors.title: LITHIUM EXPORT CONTROLS
frictionVectors.details: Harare's restrictions on unprocessed lithium exports seek to force local beneficiation, but weak power supply, financing, and processing capacity limit implementation and bargaining leverage.
